mappings.note: Why blood is sent to the kidney for filtration -- removal of nitrogenous waste from the transport medium. Human excretion pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.
The stored food of animals is glycogen. Storage of the products of nutrition, so C 3.2-LO-1; C 3.2-LO-3 is about energy released by respiration, not the reserve laid down.
How water moves at night with no transpiration -- root pressure. Plant transport, C 4.3-LO-1; deliberately the same outcome as the daytime transpiration-pull question so the pair reads as one idea.
Which food component is not digested in the stomach (carbohydrate/fat). A step-by-step digestion question, C 3.2-LO-1.
The purpose of making urine -- excreting nitrogenous waste and regulating water. Human excretion, C 3.2-LO-2.
Site of complete digestion of all three food classes -- the small intestine. C 3.2-LO-1.
Why ventricles have thicker walls than atria -- they pump blood further. Heart structure within the transport pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.
How plant cells change shape -- water entering or leaving alters turgor. This is the semi-permeable-membrane strand of C 3.1, the same mechanism as the guard-cell items.
Two enzymes in pancreatic juice -- trypsin and lipase. Human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.
Function of the alveoli -- C 4.2-LO-1 names the alveolus and its structure-to-function relation.
Form in which food energy is stored in humans (glycogen). Paired with qid:85708 and given the same outcome for the same reason.
Why the air passage does not collapse on exhaling -- cartilage rings in the trachea. An organ of the respiratory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.

The process a single-celled organism uses for food, gas exchange and waste removal is diffusion. It spans three life processes in a non-human organism, so the competency C 3.2, not any of the human-specific LOs.

Organisms using CO2 and water as food are autotrophs -- the autotrophic/heterotrophic distinction in C 3.2-LO-1. C 4.1 was considered but is about sorting organisms into five kingdoms, which is not asked.
Why we need energy even at rest -- involuntary life processes continue. Argues across all the life processes at once, so the competency C 3.2 rather than the respiration outcome LO-3.
Which blood components carry food, CO2 and wastes, and which carries oxygen. Human transport, C 3.2-LO-2.
Why cartilage rings are present in the trachea. Duplicate of qid:85718 under a different source tag; mapped to the same code.
The two ways glucose is oxidised plus two differences between them -- the aerobic/anaerobic comparison, C 3.2-LO-3.
Function of the trachea and why it does not collapse. The organ-and-pathway outcome C 3.2-LO-2; C 4.2-LO-1 is not cited because the trachea is not one of the three structures it names.

DEFECT: 'How do THEY take up carbon dioxide' has no antecedent -- the desert-plant subject was lost from the stem. The stored answer (night CO2 uptake, fixed as malic acid, Calvin cycle by day) confirms it is autotrophic nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.

Part (a), guard cells swelling when water flows in, is C 3.1. Part (b), how plants transmit information from cell to cell, is Control and Coordination content that has strayed into a Life Processes item -- this chapter's frame has no plant-coordination outcome (C 4.2-LO-3 belongs to chapter 1017 and is illegal here), so C 4.2, levels of organisation, is cited as the nearest legal home.
The different ways glucose is oxidised -- C 3.2-LO-3, same as qid:85697 and qid:85724.
What excretion is, and how unicellular organisms remove waste. Defines the process generally and then applies it outside humans, so the competency C 3.2 rather than the human-only LO-2.
The plant energy reserve is starch; animals store glycogen instead. A comparison of storage products of nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.
Significance of peristalsis along the gut -- moving food through the digestive sequence, C 3.2-LO-1.
What the amount of water reabsorbed in the nephron tubule depends on. Regulation within the human excretory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2, not the nephron-structure outcome C 4.2-LO-1.
Two digestive glands and their secretions -- liver/bile and pancreas/pancreatic juice. C 3.2-LO-1.
Which mechanism moves water by day (transpiration pull) and at night (root pressure). Plant transport, C 4.3-LO-1.

Two unrelated halves. (a) why diffusion cannot serve a large multicellular body is the body-organisation argument, C 4.2; (b) how desert plants photosynthesise with daytime-closed stomata is autotrophic nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.
What translocation is and how it happens -- phloem loading and pressure flow, C 4.3-LO-1.
Two differences between arteries and veins. Same as qid:85652; C 3.2-LO-2.
Nutrition in Amoeba. Duplicate of qid:85675; same outcome C 3.2-LO-1.
Parasitic nutrition with two examples -- a heterotrophic mode, C 3.2-LO-1.
How leakage from blood vessels is prevented -- platelet clotting. Blood within the transport system, C 3.2-LO-2.
Draw nutrition in Amoeba and name another unicellular organism. Still a heterotrophic-nutrition item, C 3.2-LO-1; drawing does not make it a CG 8 modelling task.
Vaseline-coated leaves of a potted plant. Duplicate of qid:85649 and mapped to the same competency C 3.2, because blocked stomata stop both gas exchange and transpiration.
How transpiration is useful to the plant -- water ascent, mineral delivery, cooling. C 4.3-LO-1.
The two components of the plant transport system and one function each -- xylem and phloem, C 4.3-LO-1.
Function of guard cells and what happens when water flows into them. Turgor-driven opening, the cell-level mechanism in C 3.1.
Why the nasal passage has hair and mucus, and why the throat has cartilage rings. Both are features of the human respiratory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.

Tooth enamel: its compound, the pH at which it corrodes, the role of mouth bacteria, and how to prevent decay. The assessed science is acid-base action on a salt, which is C 1.3; it sits in a digestion bank because the mouth is where nutrition begins, so C 3.2-LO-1 is cited second. Worth noting this is really Acids, Bases and Salts content.
Site of complete digestion and the end products of all three food classes -- C 3.2-LO-1.

Balanced equation for photosynthesis, and when desert plants take up CO2. Both are autotrophic nutrition (C 3.2-LO-1); the equation is not a C 1.3 citation because nothing about chemical bonding or acid-base behaviour is assessed.
Muscle cramps from sudden activity, and the respiration type in fermenting yeast. Both are anaerobic respiration and its products, C 3.2-LO-3.

Why the leaf peel is stained before glycerine is added. Laboratory procedure; cited at goal level (CG 8, exploring Science by doing Science) because its sole competency C 8.1 is about geometric, mathematical and graphical models, which a staining step is not.
Which stain is preferred and how excess is removed -- pure technique, CG 8 for the same reason as qid:85751.
Why a turgid leaf is chosen. Duplicate of qid:85627 under a different source tag; same goal-level code.
Removing excess stain and the cotton-wool outcome. Duplicate of qid:85628; same goal-level code.

Naming the two nucleated cell types seen in a leaf peel -- epidermal cells and guard cells. This asks what is OBSERVED, not how to prepare it, so it is cellular biology (C 3.1) rather than CG 8 technique.
How to obtain a transparent peel from a Rhoeo or lily leaf -- a procedural question, CG 8.

DEFECT: 'where you would expect THEM to obtain' has a dangling pronoun. The stored answer gives both a procedure (middle of the leaf, twisted and torn) and the biology behind it (stomata on the lower surface in dicots, both surfaces in monocots), so both CG 8 and C 3.1 are cited.
Shape of guard cells and what they contain (including chloroplasts) -- cellular components, C 3.1.
Two functions of the cells surrounding the stoma -- guard-cell turgor control, C 3.1.
Why a leaf is chosen for the mount (procedure, CG 8) and two functions of stomata (gas exchange and transpiration, the exchange-of-materials strand of C 3.2). Both halves are assessed.
Materials needed to prepare the temporary mount -- apparatus recall, CG 8.
Which four materials are missing from Suresh's list -- the same apparatus recall as qid:85761, CG 8.
What is seen under low and high power of the microscope. Again an observation question about cells rather than a procedure, so C 3.1 not CG 8.
Two substances selectively reabsorbed along the tubule, and where urine is stored. Human excretory pathway and its organs, C 3.2-LO-2.
Why ventricles are thicker than atria and capillary walls one cell thick. Both about vessels and chambers of the human transport system, C 3.2-LO-2.
Which cells control the stomatal pore and how -- guard cells and turgor, C 3.1.
